questions.stem: A required one-year project costing 5,000 may start in 2028 or 2029. The budgets are 4,800 in 2028 and 5,200 in 2029. What should the budget check report?

options.text: A problem, since the project overruns the 2028 budget
options.says: It fires only when every start year overruns; 2029 has room.

options.text: A problem, since the project overruns its earliest start year
options.says: The earliest year is one option of two; the check looks at all of them.

options.text: No problem, since one of its start years has room for it
options.says: Right: in 2029 the project fits on its own, so the check cannot prove there is no plan.

options.text: No problem, since only the total over all years matters
options.says: The budget rows are yearly, and the check compares the project with each year's budget.

origin.section: Each Check Reads One Project, Group or Region Against One Limit

questions.stem: A colleague proposes a floor check that adds up what last year's chosen plan spent in a region and fires when that sum is below the region's floor. What is wrong with it?

options.text: It can fire when a plan exists, since another plan may meet the floor
options.says: Right: a sound check compares the floor with the most the region could get, not with one plan.

options.text: It can miss a typed floor, since last year's plan funded every project
options.says: Funding every project would make the sum the largest possible, which is the sound version.

options.text: It forgets forced-out projects, which a floor check must add back in
options.says: A sound floor check leaves forced-out projects out of the supply, as the lesson's does.

options.text: It is too slow, since it reads every project in every region of the plan
options.says: Reading the input is cheap; the checks cost far less than a solve.

origin.section: A Check Must Never Refuse a Scenario That Has a Plan

questions.stem: A scenario passes all five pre-solve checks, but the solver still says INFEASIBLE. What does that tell you?

options.text: A check is wrong, since passing all five proves that a plan exists
options.says: Checks are sound, not complete: passing them proves nothing.

options.text: The solver is wrong, since the data has no known error left in it
options.says: INFEASIBLE is a proof; the Budget Lock scenario showed a real clash the checks cannot see.

options.text: The model has a bug, since data that passes the checks cannot clash
options.says: Rules can clash together, as the overrides and the 2028 budget did.

options.text: Several rules clash together, which only a conflict finder can name
options.says: Right: each check looks at one project, group or region; combinations need the IIS.

origin.section: Passing Every Check Does Not Mean a Plan Exists
